questions.question: Explain, using a pizza, why one half, two quarters and four eighths are equivalent.
questions.expected_answer: Cut a pizza in half and keep one half. Cut every slice into 2: the pizza has 4 slices and the half is 2 of them, two quarters. Cut every slice again: 8 slices and the half is 4 of them, four eighths. The amount of pizza never changed, only the number of slices, so the three fractions are equivalent.

questions.question: Write three quarters in eighths and two thirds in sixths, showing the multiplying.
questions.expected_answer: Three quarters: 4 times 2 is 8, so multiply the top by 2 as well, 3 times 2 is 6, giving six eighths. Two thirds: 3 times 2 is 6, and 2 times 2 is 4, giving four sixths.

questions.question: Use equivalent fractions to decide whether 3/4 or 5/8 is bigger, and explain why adding 1 to the top and bottom of 1/2 does not give an equivalent fraction.
questions.expected_answer: 3/4 is 6/8, and 6/8 is bigger than 5/8, so 3/4 is bigger. Adding 1 to top and bottom of 1/2 gives 2/3, which is more than a half on the fraction wall, so the amount changed and the fractions are not equivalent.
